children: There is another take on this common interpretation of the “Bloo… Me? No.” line. One must ask why Bloom would think those first four letters might refer to him. The “somber” young man from the Y.M.C.A. who handed tract to him would bear the obvious trappings, a religious pamphlet will clearly have that appearance, especially to an ad man like Bloom, who would detect at a glance its nature. To suggest that he would process the heading letter-by-letter, “B..L..O..O..” as if he were a young child learning to read seems beyond credibility. Perhaps the temptation to fill in the “M” is too great for readers. It is hard to conceive that he would not have seen the heading in its entirety as any experienced reader would. His reaction, “Me? No.” is more likely in response to the full heading of the tract – “Blood of the Lamb.”

Bloom continues to read in the pamphlet, “Are you saved? All are washed in the blood of the lamb. God wants blood victim. Birth, hymen, martyr, war, foundation of a building, sacrifice, kidney burntoffering, druids' altars. Elijah is coming”. While the sentence, “All are washed in the blood of the lamb,” plainly references Revelation 7:14 from the New Testament, Elijah, and the references to animal and blood sacrifice are better reflections from the Old Testament, with which, as a Jew, Bloom should have been better familiar. The most prominent imagery in Judaism may be the lamb’s blood  which the Israelites in Egypt were to “take of…, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat [the lamb].” Those who didn’t do so lost their firstborn child to the Destroying Angel. Is it not much more likely that the natural question for Leopold Bloom would have been, “Did you take of the lamb’s blood and strike it on the door posts of your house?” His answer would have been, “Me? No,” and the result was the destruction of his son, albeit not his firstborn, the fault being only his. The fact that mention of Elijah, the telling of whose future coming is a vital part of the Passover ritual, was made in tandem within this passage seems to support this contention. There are several indirect references to the Passover in Ulysses, beginning in Telemachus with bowls of bitter waters, suggesting the eating of bitter herbs, the waters also miraculously turning through Moses into blood, a major theme in Joyce’s passage here and in the freeing of the Hebrews from bondage.

5211448.fragment: Fifteen children he had. Birth every year almost. That’s in their theology or the priest won’t give the poor woman the confession, the absolution. Increase and multiply

range.content: Fifteen children he had. Birth every year almost. That's in their theology or the priest won't give the poor woman the confession, the absolution. Increase and multiply

5211448.twitter_share_message: “Bloom is referring here to how the Catholic faith denies its adherents the use of birth control,…” —@Genius

children: Bloom is referring here to how the Catholic faith denies its adherents the use of birth control, to use preventative measures would be a mortal sin.

For the Vatican, the primary purpose of intercourse was for the sacred act of procreation. If couples were interested in having intercourse, then they had to be willing to accept the potential for the creation of another life. For devout Catholics, that left only abstinence or the church-approved rhythm method (the practice of abstaining from sex during the woman’s period of ovulation).In fact the Roman Catholic Church officially banned any “artificial” means of birth control in 1930. Condoms, diaphragms and cervical caps were defined as artificial, since they blocked the natural journey of sperm during intercourse. Douches, suppositories and spermicides all killed or impeded sperm, and were banned as well. According to Church doctrine, tampering with the “male seed” was tantamount to murder. A common admonition on the subject at the time was “so many conceptions prevented, so many homicides.” To interfere with God’s will was a mortal sin and grounds for excommunication.

children: A crossbun is a pastry usually eaten hot, containing spices and raisins with a cross on the top to signify the crucifixion of Jesus. Typically eaten on Good Friday by Christians. Here Joyce contrasts two religious holidays, Yom Kippur, a day of fasting, prayer and atonement, and Good Friday. Although the Catholic Church treats Good Friday as a fast day, this is understood as having only one full meal and two collations (a smaller repast) and on which the faithful abstain from eating meat. This is why many places have the typical ‘Fish Friday’. Here again Bloom, when he says `for fear he’d collapse..‘ is implying that Catholics are unable, possibly too weak, to fast as Jews do.

8266920.twitter_share_message: “This is a classic example of James Joyce’s predilection for punning and literary ‘easter eggs.’ …” —@Genius

children: This is a classic example of James Joyce’s predilection for punning and literary ‘easter eggs.’ While on the surface this line is merely a comical, if quotidian, image, it is particularly notable for the crossing over of the “Y” and the “S” in “H.E.L.Y.S.” The first word of
Ulysses
is
“stately”
and the last Molly Bloom’s emphatic, feminine
“Yes”

, one starting with “s” and one “y.” Therefore, the “s” and the “y” must at some point cross over and here, the middle of the book, 12:00 noon, is where this happens. While this is likely meant as a simple structural nuance, perhaps not conveying any great meaning, it is nonetheless interesting to see how Joyce’s overarching scheme for the novel fits together.
